newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO meet to forge Hebron deal.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO meet to forge Hebron deal.

text.p: Israel and the PLO tried to finally wrap up their Hebron agreement on Monday after removing the main obstacle during a lightning mediation mission by Jordan's King Hussein.

A PLO official said negotiators, meeting at a Jerusalem hotel, could conclude a deal within hours thanks to a compromise reached on Sunday for Israel to complete three troop withdrawals from still-occupied West Bank areas by mid-1998.

Saeb Erekat, head of the PLO negotiating team, said "some disputes" still had to be resolved before Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat could meet to seal the deal.
"If there are no surprises, we should be able to finish today. If we do, this will pave the way for a summit," Palestinian negotiator Hassan Asfour told Reuters.
News of a possible agreement angered members of Netanyahu's right-leaning cabinet and Jewish settler leaders who want to hang on to occupied lands.
U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross, encouraged by the progress, cancelled plans to head home after a three-week mediation effort while emphasising the two sides still had disputes to resolve.

A timeframe for the pullbacks, originally due to be completed by September this year, had been the main stumbling block to Israel's handover of 80 percent of Hebron, a town holy to Moslems and Jews as the biblical Abraham's burial place.

"King Hussein, U.S. envoy Dennis Ross and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu telephoned Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and told him Netanyahu has accepted the formula," said a PLO official who asked not to be identified.

"I think because of the important initiative that His Majesty took, we have made considerable progress and I think we can envision the end of the negotiations in sight," Netanyahu said after meeting the monarch late on Sunday.

The PLO had been reluctant to sign an accord on Hebron, where some 400 Jewish settlers live in the heart of 100,000 Palestinians, without a commitment from Israel to carry out the additional West Bank pullbacks agreed in previous peace deals.

Israel had proposed to complete the West Bank pullbacks by May 1999 and the United States suggested 1998. The PLO demanded Israel stick to a 1995 peace deal signed by Israel's previous left-leaning government under which the withdrawals were to have been completed by September this year.
Under the compromise, proposed by Egypt and Jordan and pushed by the king on Sunday, the withdrawals will be completed by sometime in mid-1998, PLO officials said.
Arafat scheduled a meeting of both his cabinet and the PLO executive committee for 1700 GMT. His spokesman said the Palestinian leader would brief them on peace moves.
At least seven ministers on Netanyahu's 18-member cabinet were expected to oppose the deal.
"This is very severe in our eyes. I doubt the prime minister will obtain a majority," said Transport Minister Yigal Bibi of the National Religious Party.
Jewish settlers called an "emergency meeting" and warned that an Israeli withdrawal would lead to bloodshed.

"The agreement is liable to create an extremely severe and dangerous situation here," said Noam Arnon, spokesman for the Hebron settlers. The West Bank town has been a flashpoint for Arab-Israeli violence.
King Hussein discussed the compromise during talks on Sunday in Gaza with Arafat and by telephone with Egyptian leader Hosni Mubarak. The king then flew to Tel Aviv to see Netanyahu.
